paras: The police shooting of Jim Cullins took place on the night of 24 August 1895 in Lynchburg, Virginia, when Police Officer J. R. Coomes shot Cullins, a Black man, during an attempted arrest. Two of four shots struck Cullins, who was reported "probably fatally wounded," though no later report of his death or recovery was found.

According to a Lynchburg dispatch printed in the Richmond Times, Coomes was trying to arrest Cullins on a foot bridge in the city. The dispatch said Cullins "resisted arrest" and struck the officer in the face with what was "thought" to be "a pair of knucks," then tried to throw him over the railing of the bridge. Coomes then fired four times, and two of the balls hit Cullins.
The report did not say why Coomes was arresting Cullins, and it gave no account from Cullins or any witness.
No report of an inquest, hearing or charge against either man appears in the coverage, and Cullins's condition after the night of the shooting is not recorded.

The only known report ran on the front page of the Richmond Times on 25 August 1895 under the headline "ASSAULTED A POLICEMAN." Its subheading, "A Negro Perhaps Fatally Wounded While Resisting a Lynchburg Officer," placed Cullins's alleged resistance at the center of the story and presented the officer's version as fact. The dispatch called Cullins "a colored man" and "the negro," while naming the officer with his title and initials.
No coverage of the shooting was found in the Black press or in other white newspapers during August and September 1895.
